claim: Antibiotics of the β-lactam (penicillin) family inactivate target enzymes called D,D-transpeptidases or penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs) that catalyze the last cross-linking step of peptidoglycan synthesis.
source: Antibiotics of the β-lactam (penicillin) family inactivate target enzymes called D,D-transpeptidases or penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs) that catalyze the last cross-linking step of peptidoglycan synthesis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about β-lactam antibiotics and their mechanism of action.

claim: The peptidoglycan is a net-like macromolecule that is the essential component of bacterial cell walls that sustains the osmotic pressure of the cytoplasm.
source: The resulting net-like macromolecule is the essential component of bacterial cell walls that sustains the osmotic pressure of the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is established knowledge about peptidoglycan structure and function.

claim: In Escherichia coli, bypass of PBPs by the YcbB L,D-transpeptidase leads to resistance to β-lactam drugs.
source: In Escherichia coli, bypass of PBPs by the YcbB L,D-transpeptidase leads to resistance to these drugs.
evidence: This is a key finding from previous work that motivates the current study.

claim: PBPs and YcbB similarly participated in single-strand insertion of glycan chains into the expanding bacterial side wall.
source: PBPs and YcbB similarly participated in single-strand insertion of glycan chains into the expanding bacterial side wall.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on the isotope labeling experiments.

claim: The absence of any transpeptidase-specific signature suggests that the peptidoglycan expansion mode is determined by other components of polymerization complexes.
source: This absence of any transpeptidase-specific signature suggests that the peptidoglycan expansion mode is determined by other components of polymerization complexes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that PBPs and YcbB show similar insertion patterns.

claim: YcbB mediated β-lactam resistance by insertion of multiple strands that were exclusively cross-linked to existing tripeptide-containing acceptors.
source: YcbB did mediate β-lactam resistance by insertion of multiple strands that were exclusively cross-linked to existing tripeptide-containing acceptors.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on analysis of peptidoglycan in the presence of ampicillin.

claim: The mode of polymerization by YcbB in the presence of β-lactams depends upon accumulation of linear glycan chains due to PBP inactivation, formation of tripeptides due to cleavage of existing cross-links by a β-lactam-insensitive endopeptidase, and concerted cross-linking by YcbB.
source: We propose that this undocumented mode of polymerization depends upon accumulation of linear glycan chains due to PBP inactivation, formation of tripeptides due to cleavage of existing cross-links by a β-lactam-insensitive endopeptidase, and concerted cross-linking by YcbB.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental observations.

claim: The peptidoglycan determines the shape of bacterial cells and is intimately integrated into the cell division process.
source: The peptidoglycan also determines the shape of bacterial cells and is intimately integrated into the cell division process since the barrier to the osmotic pressure needs to be maintained during the entire cell cycle.
evidence: This is established knowledge about peptidoglycan function.

claim: The peptidoglycan is assembled from disaccharide-peptide subunits consisting of β,1→4 linked N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc) and N-acetyl muramic acid (MurNAc) and a stem peptide linked to the D-lactoyl group of MurNAc.
source: It is assembled from disaccharide-peptide subunits consisting of β,1→4 linked N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc) and N-acetyl muramic acid (MurNAc) and a stem peptide linked to the D-lactoyl group of MurNAc (Figure 1B; Mengin-Lecreulx et al., 1982).
evidence: This is established knowledge about peptidoglycan structure, supported by citation.

claim: Polymerization of the peptidoglycan subunit is mediated by glycosyltransferases for the elongation of glycan chains and by transpeptidases for cross-linking stem peptides carried by adjacent glycan chains.
source: Polymerization of the subunit is mediated by glycosyltransferases for the elongation of glycan chains and by transpeptidases for cross-linking stem peptides carried by adjacent glycan chains.
evidence: This is established knowledge about peptidoglycan biosynthesis.

claim: PBPs catalyze the formation of 4→3 cross-links connecting the carbonyl of D-Ala at the 4th position of an acyl donor stem peptide to the side-chain amino group of DAP at the 3rd position of an acyl acceptor stem peptide.
source: Active-site Ser transpeptidases belonging to the penicillin-binding protein (PBP) family catalyze the formation of 4→3 cross-links connecting the carbonyl of D-Ala at the 4th position of an acyl donor stem peptide to the side-chain amino group of DAP (D stereo-center) at the 3rd position of an acyl acceptor stem peptide.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PBP activity, illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: LDTs catalyze the formation of 3→3 cross-links connecting two DAP residues.
source: Active-site Cys transpeptidases belonging to the L,D-transpeptidase (LDT) family catalyze the formation of 3→3 cross-links connecting two DAP residues.
evidence: This is established knowledge about LDT activity, illustrated in Figure 1D.

claim: A pentapeptide stem is essential in the donor substrate for PBPs to form the acyl enzyme intermediate.
source: A pentapeptide stem is essential in the donor substrate to form the acyl enzyme intermediate.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PBP substrate specificity.

claim: LDTs are specific of tetrapeptide-containing donors.
source: LDTs are specific of tetrapeptide-containing donors.
evidence: This is established knowledge about LDT substrate specificity.

claim: PBPs are inactivated by all classes of β-lactams, whereas LDTs are inactivated by carbapenems only.
source: PBPs are inactivated by all classes of β-lactams, whereas LDTs are inactivated by carbapenems only (Mainardi et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: In wild-type Escherichia coli, LDTs are fully dispensable for growth, at least in laboratory conditions.
source: In wild-type Escherichia coli, LDTs are fully dispensable for growth, at least in laboratory conditions (Magnet et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: LDTs have a minor contribution to peptidoglycan cross-linking in the exponential growth phase in wild-type E. coli.
source: Accordingly, these enzymes have a minor contribution to peptidoglycan cross-linking in the exponential growth phase (Vollmer and Bertsche, 2008; Glauner, 1988).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Selection of mutants resistant to ceftriaxone results in a full bypass of PBPs by the YcbB LDT.
source: However, selection of mutants resistant to ceftriaxone, a β-lactam of the cephalosporin class, results in a full bypass of PBPs by the YcbB LDT (Hugonnet et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous work, supported by citation.

claim: The bypass of PBPs by YcbB requires overproduction of both the (p)ppGpp alarmone and YcbB.
source: The bypass requires overproduction of both the (p)ppGpp alarmone and YcbB.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous work.

claim: The peptidoglycan of the ceftriaxone-resistant mutant grown in the presence of ceftriaxone only contains 3→3 cross-links following PBP inhibition.
source: The peptidoglycan of the mutant grown in the presence of ceftriaxone only contains 3→3 cross-links following PBP inhibition.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous work.

claim: DDCs hydrolyze the D-Ala4-D-Ala5 amide bond of stem pentapeptides to generate stem tetrapeptides in mature peptidoglycan.
source: DDCs, which belong to the PBP family, hydrolyze the D-Ala4-D-Ala5 amide bond of stem pentapeptides to generate stem tetrapeptides in mature peptidoglycan (Sauvage et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The DDC reaction is nearly total in E. coli, so stem pentapeptides are found in very low abundance unless DDCs are inactivated by β-lactams.
source: Since the reaction is nearly total in E. coli, stem pentapeptides are found in very low abundance unless DDCs are inactivated by β-lactams.
evidence: This is established knowledge about E. coli peptidoglycan metabolism.

claim: The L,D-carboxypeptidase activity of LDTs hydrolyzes the DAP3-D-Ala4 amide bond generating tripeptide stems from tetrapeptide stems.
source: The L,D-carboxypeptidase activity of LDTs hydrolyzes the DAP3-D-Ala4 amide bond generating tripeptide stems from tetrapeptide stems (Magnet et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The peptidoglycan contains combinations of tripeptide and tetrapeptide stems in monomers and in the acyl acceptor position of dimers because the L,D-carboxypeptidase reaction is incomplete.
source: Since this reaction is incomplete the peptidoglycan contains combinations of tripeptide and tetrapeptide stems in monomers and in the acyl acceptor position of dimers.
evidence: This is an inference based on the incomplete nature of the L,D-carboxypeptidase reaction.

claim: DDCs eliminate the essential pentapeptide donor of PBPs and generate the essential tetrapeptide donor of LDTs by removing D-Ala5 from pentapeptide stems.
source: By removing D-Ala5 from pentapeptide stems, DDCs eliminate the essential pentapeptide donor of PBPs and generate the essential tetrapeptide donor of LDTs (Mainardi et al., 2002; Hugonnet et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: LDCs eliminate the essential tetrapeptide donor of LDTs by removing D-Ala4 from tetrapeptide stems, thereby potentially limiting the formation of 3→3 cross-links.
source: By removing D-Ala4 from tetrapeptide stems, LDCs eliminate the essential tetrapeptide donor of LDTs thereby potentially limiting the formation of 3→3 cross-links.
evidence: This is an inference based on the substrate specificity of LDTs.

claim: DDC and LDC activities control both the extent of peptidoglycan cross-linking and the relative contributions of D,D-transpeptidases and LDTs to peptidoglycan cross-linking.
source: Thus, DDC and LDC activities control both the extent of peptidoglycan cross-linking and the relative contributions of D,D-transpeptidases and LDTs to peptidoglycan cross-linking.
evidence: This is an inference based on the roles of DDCs and LDCs in generating and eliminating transpeptidase substrates.

claim: Endopeptidases cleave cross-links in peptidoglycan.
source: The interconversion between monomers and cross-linked dimers involves not only PBPs and LDTs in the biosynthetic direction but also hydrolytic enzymes, referred to as endopeptidases, which cleave the cross-links.
evidence: This is established knowledge about peptidoglycan metabolism.

claim: Endopeptidases belonging to the PBP family are specific of 4→3 cross-links whereas other endopeptidases cleave both 4→3 and 3→3 cross-links.
source: Endopeptidases belonging to the PBP family are specific of 4→3 cross-links whereas other endopeptidases cleave both 4→3 and 3→3 cross-links (Voedts et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Among eight endopeptidases with partially redundant functions, at least one enzyme is essential in the context of the formation of 4→3 cross-links.
source: Among eight endopeptidases with partially redundant functions, at least one enzyme is essential in the context of the formation of 4→3 cross-links whereas two endopeptidases, MepM and MepK, are required in the context of 3→3 cross-links (Voedts et al., 2021; Singh et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Two endopeptidases, MepM and MepK, are required in the context of 3→3 cross-links.
source: Among eight endopeptidases with partially redundant functions, at least one enzyme is essential in the context of the formation of 4→3 cross-links whereas two endopeptidases, MepM and MepK, are required in the context of 3→3 cross-links (Voedts et al., 2021; Singh et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Morphogenesis of E. coli cells depends upon controlled expansion of the peptidoglycan and requires scaffolding proteins, actin (MreB) and tubulin (FtsZ) homologues.
source: Morphogenesis of E. coli cells depends upon controlled expansion of the peptidoglycan and requires scaffolding proteins, actin (MreB) and tubulin (FtsZ) homologues (den Blaauwen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Scaffolding proteins are involved in the recruitment of peptidoglycan polymerases and in the coordination of their activities with that of hydrolases.
source: These proteins are involved in the recruitment of peptidoglycan polymerases and in the coordination of their activities with that of hydrolases (Vollmer and Höltje, 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The E. coli cell cycle involves two phases: the MreB-dependent elongation of the side wall at a constant diameter and the FtsZ-dependent formation of the septum at mid-cell.
source: The cell cycle involves two phases, namely the MreB-dependent elongation of the side wall at a constant diameter and the FtsZ-dependent formation of the septum at mid-cell.
evidence: This is established knowledge about E. coli cell division.

claim: Cell wall synthesis processes are thought to involve two distinct multienzyme complexes, the elongasome and the divisome, and specific enzymes, in particular class B PBP2 and PBP3.
source: These processes are thought to involve two distinct multienzyme complexes, the elongasome and the divisome, and specific enzymes, in particular class B PBP2 and PBP3, which mediate peptidoglycan cross-linking in the side wall and in the septum, respectively (Höltje, 1996).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Specific inactivation of PBP2 by mecillinam results in the growth of E. coli as spheres.
source: Accordingly, specific inactivation of PBP2 by mecillinam or of PBP3 by aztreonam results in the growth of E. coli as spheres or as filaments, respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the effects of specific PBP inhibition.

claim: Specific inactivation of PBP3 by aztreonam results in the growth of E. coli as filaments.
source: Accordingly, specific inactivation of PBP2 by mecillinam or of PBP3 by aztreonam results in the growth of E. coli as spheres or as filaments, respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the effects of specific PBP inhibition.

claim: Most models propose a regular arrangement of glycan strands parallel to the cell surface and perpendicular to the long axis of the cell.
source: Most models propose a regular arrangement of glycan strands parallel to the cell surface and perpendicular to the long axis of the cell as depicted in Figure 1A; Typas et al., 2011.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: It has been proposed that the glycan strands protrude perpendicularly to the surface of the cytoplasmic membrane.
source: Alternatively, it has been proposed that the glycan strands protrude perpendicularly to the surface of the cytoplasmic membrane (Meroueh et al., 2006; Dmitriev et al., 2003).
evidence: This is an alternative model from the literature, supported by citations.

claim: The lack of direct experimental evidence for peptidoglycan structure originates from the heterogeneity of the peptidoglycan macromolecule that prevents the analysis of the polymer by radiocrystallography.
source: The lack of direct experimental evidence originates from the heterogeneity of the peptidoglycan macromolecule that prevents the analysis of the polymer by radiocrystallography.
evidence: This is an explanation for the lack of structural data on peptidoglycan.

claim: NMR spectroscopy failed to determine the precise and complete structure of peptidoglycan due to its heterogeneity and its important flexibility.
source: NMR spectroscopy also failed to determine the precise and complete structure of the polymer due to its heterogeneity and its important flexibility, as measured by solid-state NMR relaxation (Kern et al., 2008; Sharif et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: According to the 'three-for-one' model, peptidoglycan expansion involves the insertion of three neo-synthesized glycan strands to the detriment of the hydrolysis of one existing strand, which acts as a docking strand.
source: According to the 'three-for-one' model, peptidoglycan expansion involves the insertion of three neo-synthesized glycan strands to the detriment of the hydrolysis of one existing strand, which acts as a docking strand (Vollmer and Höltje, 2001).
evidence: This is an established model from the literature, supported by citation.

claim: Glycan strands may be inserted according either to a 'one-at-a-time' model or a 'two-at-a-time' model.
source: Alternatively, glycan strands may be inserted according either to a 'one-at-a-time' model or a 'two-at-a-time' model, the latter being supported by the dimeric nature of certain D,D-transpeptidases (Charpentier et al., 2002).
evidence: These are alternative models from the literature, with the two-at-a-time model supported by citation.

claim: All peptidoglycan expansion models postulate that peptidoglycan expansion requires cleavage of cross-links by endopeptidases.
source: All these models postulate that peptidoglycan expansion requires cleavage of cross-links by endopeptidases and obey to the 'make-before-break' principle, which proposes that cross-links in the existing peptidoglycan are hydrolyzed by endopeptidases only if the newly synthesized glycan strands are cross-linked and can sustain the osmotic pressure of the cytoplasm (Vollmer and Höltje, 2001).
evidence: This is a common feature of established models, supported by citation.

claim: The 'make-before-break' principle proposes that cross-links in the existing peptidoglycan are hydrolyzed by endopeptidases only if the newly synthesized glycan strands are cross-linked and can sustain the osmotic pressure of the cytoplasm.
source: All these models postulate that peptidoglycan expansion requires cleavage of cross-links by endopeptidases and obey to the 'make-before-break' principle, which proposes that cross-links in the existing peptidoglycan are hydrolyzed by endopeptidases only if the newly synthesized glycan strands are cross-linked and can sustain the osmotic pressure of the cytoplasm (Vollmer and Höltje, 2001).
evidence: This is an established principle from the literature, supported by citation.

claim: At each generation, about half of the disaccharide-peptide units is released from the peptidoglycan by the combined action of endopeptidases and lytic transglycosylases.
source: At each generation, about half of the disaccharide-peptide units is released from the peptidoglycan by the combined action of endopeptidases and lytic transglycosylases (Goodell, 1985a; Johnson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Lytic transglycosylases catalyze a non-hydrolytic cleavage of the β,1→4 MurNAc-GlcNAc glycosydic bond and generate GlcNAc-anhydro-MurNAc-peptides fragments via MurNAc cyclisation at positions 1 and 6.
source: The latter enzymes catalyze a non-hydrolytic cleavage of the β,1→4 MurNAc-GlcNAc glycosydic bond and generate GlcNAc-anhydro-MurNAc-peptides fragments via MurNAc cyclisation at positions 1 and 6.
evidence: This is established knowledge about lytic transglycosylase activity.

claim: Peptidoglycan fragments are transported into the cytoplasm by the AmpG permease and recycled.
source: These fragments are transported into the cytoplasm by the AmpG permease and recycled according to the pathway depicted in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.
evidence: This is established knowledge illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The L-Ala-γ-D-Glu-DAP tripeptide is directly recycled in the peptidoglycan recycling pathway.
source: The key features of the recycling pathway are that the L-Ala-γ-D-Glu-DAP tripeptide is directly recycled whereas the glucosamine moiety of GlcNAc and MurNAc reenters into the peptidoglycan biosynthesis pathway at the level of glucosamine-6-phosphate.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the peptidoglycan recycling pathway.

claim: The glucosamine moiety of GlcNAc and MurNAc reenters into the peptidoglycan biosynthesis pathway at the level of glucosamine-6-phosphate.
source: The key features of the recycling pathway are that the L-Ala-γ-D-Glu-DAP tripeptide is directly recycled whereas the glucosamine moiety of GlcNAc and MurNAc reenters into the peptidoglycan biosynthesis pathway at the level of glucosamine-6-phosphate.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the peptidoglycan recycling pathway.

claim: The 'three-for-one' growth model predicts that the docking strand is recycled.
source: The 'three-for-one' growth model predicts that the docking strand is recycled; conversely, the 'one-at-a-time' and 'two-at-a-time' models do not imply that recycling is a consequence of peptidoglycan synthesis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the three-for-one model.

claim: The 'one-at-a-time' and 'two-at-a-time' models do not imply that recycling is a consequence of peptidoglycan synthesis.
source: The 'three-for-one' growth model predicts that the docking strand is recycled; conversely, the 'one-at-a-time' and 'two-at-a-time' models do not imply that recycling is a consequence of peptidoglycan synthesis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the one-at-a-time and two-at-a-time models.

claim: The peptidoglycan expansion models imply specific acceptor-to-donor radioactivity ratios (ADRR) in cross-linked stem peptides.
source: The peptidoglycan expansion models described above were previously investigated by pulse labeling of peptidoglycan with radioactive DAP. Indeed, the models imply specific acceptor-to-donor radioactivity ratios (ADRR) in cross-linked stem peptides (Figure 1—figure supplement 2; de Jonge et al., 1989).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous work, supported by citation and illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The radioactive DAP labeling method is intrinsically inaccurate since newly synthesized subunits issued from the recycling of stem peptides are mistakenly identified as material from the existing wall.
source: This method is intrinsically inaccurate since newly synthesized subunits issued from the recycling of stem peptides are mistakenly identified as material from the existing wall.
evidence: This is a limitation of the radioactive DAP method identified by the authors.

claim: The radioactive DAP method provides access to the average composition of dimers in labeled donor and acceptor stems rather than the labeling status of stem peptides that have directly participated in the same cross-linking reaction.
source: Moreover, the method provides access to the average composition of dimers in labeled donor and acceptor stems rather than the labeling status of stem peptides that have directly participated in the same cross-linking reaction.
evidence: This is a limitation of the radioactive DAP method identified by the authors.

claim: The new method based on full labeling with stable isotopes combined with high-resolution mass spectrometry enables a thorough investigation of peptidoglycan synthesis and recycling in a single experiment.
source: Here, we describe a new method based on the full labeling of the entire peptidoglycan macromolecule with stable isotopes of carbon and nitrogen combined with high-resolution mass spectrometry (MS). This method does not suffer from the limitations listed above and our results show that it enables a thorough investigation of peptidoglycan synthesis and recycling in a single experiment.
evidence: This is a primary claim about the new method developed in this study.

claim: Strain M1.5 was chosen for initial experiments because D,D-transpeptidases and LDTs both have major contributions to peptidoglycan polymerization.
source: Strain M1.5 was chosen for initial experiments because D,D-transpeptidases and LDTs both have major contributions to peptidoglycan polymerization offering the possibility to study 4→3 and 3→3 cross-linked dimers from the same peptidoglycan preparation.
evidence: This is an explanation for the experimental design choice.

claim: Growth in the labeled versus unlabeled medium did not alter the muropeptide composition of peptidoglycan.
source: As expected, growth in the labeled versus unlabeled medium did not alter the muropeptide composition of peptidoglycan.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments.

claim: The mass spectra of monomers from E. coli grown in unlabeled M9 minimal medium displayed the conventional isotopic clusters as expected for the natural abundances of carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, and oxygen isotopes.
source: The mass spectra of monomers from E. coli grown in unlabeled M9 minimal medium displayed the conventional isotopic clusters (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1 for the disaccharide-tripeptide and -tetrapeptide, respectively), as expected for the natural abundances of carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, and oxygen isotopes (see Supplementary Materials and methods for the method used to deduce the mass and abundance of isotopologues from the isotopic composition of the medium).
evidence: This is an observation from MS analysis, illustrated in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The overlay of the experimental and simulated spectra confirmed the expected isotopologue composition for unlabeled muropeptides.
source: The overlay of the experimental and simulated spectra (Figure 2C) confirmed the expected isotopologue composition (see Supplementary Materials and methods for the method used to simulate mass spectra by using the deduced mass and abundance of isotopologues).
evidence: This is a validation of the MS analysis method, illustrated in Figure 2C.

claim: Extensive peptidoglycan labeling was successfully achieved, only limited by the extent (99%) of the labeling of glucose and NH4Cl introduced in the labeled growth medium.
source: Taken together, these results show that we successfully achieved extensive peptidoglycan labeling that was only limited by the extent (99%) of the labeling of glucose and NH4Cl introduced in the labeled growth medium.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the MS analysis of labeled muropeptides.

claim: Isotopic dilution due to atmospheric N2 and CO2 was not an issue for peptidoglycan labeling.
source: Thus, isotopic dilution due to atmospheric N2 and CO2 was not an issue, as expected from the metabolic fluxes of E. coli grown in minimal medium.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observed extent of labeling.

claim: Simulation of high-resolution mass spectra was successfully used to assign isotopologues of defined structure and isotopic composition to the corresponding peaks in experimental mass spectra.
source: Simulation of high-resolution mass spectra was successfully used to assign isotopologues of defined structure and isotopic composition to the corresponding peaks in experimental mass spectra (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a methodological conclusion, illustrated in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The assignments of isotopologues were confirmed by MS/MS.
source: These assignments were confirmed by MS/MS (shown for two isotopologues in Table 1).
evidence: This is a validation of the isotopologue assignments using MS/MS data shown in Table 1.

claim: The Tri→Tetra and Tetra→Tri isomers formed by YcbB and the D,D-transpeptidases can be discriminated by MS/MS on the basis of the cleavage of the DAP3→DAP3 and D-Ala4→DAP3 cross-links, respectively, and of the loss of a C-terminal D-Ala only present in the acceptor stem of the dimer generated by YcbB.
source: The Tri→Tetra and Tetra→Tri isomers formed by YcbB and the D,D-transpeptidases can be discriminated by MS/MS on the basis of the cleavage of the DAP3→DAP3 and D-Ala4→DAP3 cross-links, respectively, and of the loss of a C-terminal D-Ala only present in the acceptor stem of the dimer generated by YcbB (Supplementary data).
evidence: This is a methodological capability demonstrated by MS/MS analysis.

claim: The relative abundance of the six predominant muropeptides remained similar in all samples indicating that the medium switch did not alter the overall peptidoglycan composition.
source: The relative abundance of these six muropeptides remained similar in all samples indicating, as expected, that the medium switch did not alter the overall peptidoglycan composition.
evidence: This is an observation from the kinetic experiments.

claim: Growth in the unlabeled medium after the switch led to the appearance of disaccharide-tripeptide isotopologues of natural isotopic composition.
source: MS revealed that growth in the unlabeled medium after the switch led to the appearance of disaccharide-tripeptide isotopologues of natural isotopic composition (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is an observation from MS analysis, illustrated in Figure 4A.

claim: Minor amounts of hybrids containing both labeled and unlabeled moieties were detected after the medium switch.
source: In addition, minor amounts of hybrids containing both labeled and unlabeled moieties were detected (named h1, h2, and h3 in Figure 4A).
evidence: This is an observation from MS analysis, illustrated in Figure 4A.

claim: Hybrid h1 consists of two types of isotopologues containing a labeled hexosamine moiety either in the GlcNAc or MurNAc residue.
source: MS/MS (Supplementary file 2) indicated that hybrid h1 consists of two types of isotopologues containing a labeled hexosamine moiety either in the GlcNAc or MurNAc residue.
evidence: This is a structural determination based on MS/MS analysis.

claim: Hybrid h2 contained a labeled stem peptide and an unlabeled disaccharide.
source: Hybrid h2 contained a labeled stem peptide and an unlabeled disaccharide.
evidence: This is a structural determination based on MS/MS analysis.

claim: Hybrid h3 was uniformly labeled except for GlcNAc.
source: Hybrid h3 was uniformly labeled except for GlcNAc.
evidence: This is a structural determination based on MS/MS analysis.

claim: The structures of h1 and h2 were fully accounted for by the known peptidoglycan recycling pathway of E. coli.
source: The structures of h1 and h2 were fully accounted for by the known peptidoglycan recycling pathway of E. coli (Johnson et al., 2013; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the hybrid structures based on known metabolic pathways, supported by citation and illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The formation of the h3 hybrid did not depend upon recycling since MurNAc-peptide moieties are not selectively recycled as single molecules.
source: In contrast, the formation of the h3 hybrid did not depend upon recycling since MurNAc-peptide moieties are not selectively recycled as single molecules.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structure of h3 and knowledge of the recycling pathway.

claim: The h3 hybrid originated from moieties that were assembled after (unlabeled GlcNAc) or prior to (labeled MurNAc-peptide) the medium switch.
source: Thus, the h3 hybrid originated from moieties that were assembled after (unlabeled GlcNAc) or prior to (labeled MurNAc-peptide) the medium switch.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structure of h3.

claim: The cytoplasm of E. coli contains an important pool of UDP-MurNAc-pentapeptide (an estimate of 120,000 molecules per bacterial cell), which represents ca. 3% of the total number of disaccharide-peptide units present in the cell wall.
source: Our results are consistent with the fact that the cytoplasm of E. coli contains an important pool of UDP-MurNAc-pentapeptide (an estimate of 120,000 molecules per bacterial cell), which represents ca. 3% of the total number of disaccharide-peptide units present in the cell wall (Mengin-Lecreulx et al., 1982).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: h3 is the sole hybrid to be assembled independently from recycling.
source: These observations indicate that h3 is the sole hybrid to be assembled independently from recycling.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the analysis of hybrid structures and the ampG deletion mutant.

claim: In the ΔampG mutant, h1 hybrids were not detected, indicating that they originated from incorporation of recycled glucosamine.
source: In this mutant, h1 hybrids were not detected, indicating that they originated from incorporation of recycled glucosamine (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the analysis of the ampG deletion mutant, illustrated in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Hybrids h2 and h3 were present in the peptidoglycan of the ΔampG mutant.
source: Hybrids h2 and h3 were present in the peptidoglycan of the ΔampG mutant as expected from the metabolic chart presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.
evidence: This is an observation from the ampG deletion mutant, consistent with the metabolic pathway illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Deletion of the ampG gene is expected to reduce rather than abolish formation of the h2 hybrid.
source: Indeed, recycling of the tripeptide (hybrid h2) involves both the transport of anhydroMurNAc-peptides by AmpG and the transport of the tripeptide by the Opp permease (Johnson et al., 2013). Deletion of the ampG gene is therefore expected to reduce rather than abolish formation of the h2 hybrid.
evidence: This is an inference based on knowledge of the recycling pathway, supported by citation.

claim: The ampG deletion did not prevent formation of the h3 hybrid.
source: The h3 hybrid was proposed to originate from existing UDP-MurNAc-pentapeptide and de novo-synthesized GlcNAc moieties (above). Accordingly, the ampG deletion did not prevent formation of the h3 hybrid.
evidence: This is an observation from the ampG deletion mutant, consistent with the proposed origin of h3.

claim: Analysis of the disaccharide-tetrapeptide revealed a pattern of incorporation of unlabeled moieties very similar to that described for the disaccharide-tripeptide.
source: Analysis of the disaccharide-tetrapeptide (Figure 4B and Supplementary file 2) revealed a pattern of incorporation of unlabeled moieties very similar to that described above for the disaccharide-tripeptide.
evidence: This is an observation from MS analysis, illustrated in Figure 4B.

claim: The hybrid tetrapeptide stem present in h2 is in full agreement with the E. coli recycling pathway, as the tripeptide and the terminal D-Ala are expected to have different origins.
source: The hybrid tetrapeptide stem present in h2 is in full agreement with the E. coli recycling pathway, as the tripeptide and the terminal D-Ala are expected to have different origins.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on knowledge of the recycling pathway.

claim: For the disaccharide-tripeptide, replacement of the uniformly labeled isotopologue by its unlabeled counterpart reached ca. 50% in 85 min.
source: For the disaccharide-tripeptide, replacement of the uniformly labeled isotopologue by its unlabeled counterpart reached ca. 50% in 85 min (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the kinetic analysis, illustrated in Figure 5B.

claim: The replacement of labeled by unlabeled disaccharide-tetrapeptide was more rapid (ca. 94% in 85 min) than for the disaccharide-tripeptide.
source: In contrast, the replacement was more rapid for the disaccharide-tetrapeptide (ca. 94% in 85 min) (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the kinetic analysis, illustrated in Figure 5D.

claim: The isotopic labeling method resolved different kinetics of accumulation of the newly synthesized monomers although their relative proportions in the peptidoglycan remained similar.
source: Thus, the isotopic labeling method resolved different kinetics of accumulation of the newly synthesized monomers (Figure 5) although their relative proportions in the peptidoglycan remained similar (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparison of kinetic data (Figure 5) and compositional data (Figure 3).

claim: The sequential nature of DDC and L,D-carboxypeptidase reactions may explain the delayed accumulation of the disaccharide-tripeptide, as it derives from the disaccharide-tetrapeptide.
source: The tetrapeptide and tripeptide stems may originate from sequential hydrolytic reactions involving the removal of D-Ala5 from free (uncross-linked) pentapeptide stems by DDCs, followed by the removal of D-Ala4 from the resulting tetrapeptide by the L,D-carboxypeptidase activity of YcbB (Magnet et al., 2008). The sequential nature of these reactions may explain, at least in part, the delayed accumulation of the disaccharide-tripeptide, as it derives from the disaccharide-tetrapeptide.
evidence: This is an inference based on knowledge of the enzymatic reactions and the observed kinetics.

claim: Hybrids h1 and h2, which originated from peptidoglycan recycling, were virtually absent at 5 min and increased between 5 and 85 min for the disaccharide-tripeptide and between 5 and 30 min for the disaccharide-tetrapeptide.
source: Kinetics of accumulation of hybrids revealed that hybrids h1 and h2, which originated from peptidoglycan recycling, were virtually absent at 5 min and increased between 5 and 85 min for the disaccharide-tripeptide and between 5 and 30 min for the disaccharide-tetrapeptide (Figure 5).
evidence: This is an observation from the kinetic analysis, illustrated in Figure 5.

claim: The kinetics of h1 and h2 hybrids is expected since recycled building blocks originated from a peptidoglycan that was fully labeled at the time of the medium switch and remained partially labeled during the time course of the experiment.
source: This is expected since recycled building blocks (glucosamine and tripeptide for h1 and h2, respectively) originated from a peptidoglycan that was fully labeled at the time of the medium switch and remained partially labeled during the time course of the experiment.
evidence: This is an explanation for the observed kinetics based on the recycling pathway.

claim: h3 hybrids were already present at 5 min, and reached a maximum at ca. 18 and 30 min for tetrapeptide and tripeptide, respectively.
source: In contrast, h3 hybrids were already present at 5 min, and reached a maximum at ca. 18 and 30 min for tetrapeptide and tripeptide, respectively, as expected for their synthesis from a cytoplasmic pool of labeled UDP-MurNAc-pentapeptide present at the time of the medium switch.
evidence: This is an observation from the kinetic analysis, with an explanation based on the UDP-MurNAc-pentapeptide pool.

claim: Three main types of isotopologues were observed after the medium switch for each of the four dimers: uniformly labeled (old→old), new→old, and new→new.
source: Three main types of isotopologues were observed after the medium switch for each of the four dimers (Figure 6 for the Tri→Tri dimer and Figure 6—figure supplements 1–3 for the Tetra→Tri, Tri→Tetra, Tetra→Tetra dimer, respectively). The first type of isotopologues were uniformly labeled. These dimers were generated by the cross-linking of stem peptides assembled before the medium switch. Thus, they correspond to fragments of the existing peptidoglycan. These dimers are referred to as old→old isotopologue dimers. The second type of isotopologues was generated by the cross-linking of a donor stem assembled after the medium switch to an acceptor stem assembled prior to the medium switch (referred as new→old isotopologue dimers). These isotopologue dimers correspond to a de novo synthesized donor stem attached to the existing peptidoglycan, which provided the acceptor. The third type of dimers was generated by the cross-linking of two neo-synthesized stem peptides (new→new).
evidence: This is an observation from MS analysis, illustrated in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplements 1–3.

claim: The absence of old→new dimers indicated that the peptide stems present in the existing peptidoglycan were not used as donors for cross-linking to neo-synthesized acceptors.
source: The absence of old→new dimers (see Supplementary file 2 for MS/MS analyses) indicated that the peptide stems present in the existing peptidoglycan were not used as donors for cross-linking to neo-synthesized acceptors.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on MS/MS analysis.

claim: For 4→3 cross-linked dimers, the absence of old→new dimers is expected since D,D-transpeptidases use pentapeptide-containing donors, which are almost completely absent from mature peptidoglycan due to the hydrolysis of the D-Ala4-D-Ala5 amide bond by DDCs.
source: For 4→3 cross-linked dimers, this result is expected since D,D-transpeptidases belonging to the PBP family use pentapeptide-containing donors, which are almost completely absent from mature peptidoglycan due to the hydrolysis of the D-Ala4-D-Ala5 amide bond by DDCs (See Introduction section and Figure 1).
evidence: This is an explanation based on established knowledge about PBP substrate specificity and DDC activity.

claim: The absence of old→new 3→3 cross-linked Tri→Tetra dimer indicates that YcbB discriminates neo-synthesized tetrapeptide stems (used as donors) from existing tetrapeptide stems (used as acceptors) by an unknown mechanism.
source: For the 3→3 cross-linked Tri→Tetra dimer, tetrapeptide stems present in the existing peptidoglycan could potentially be used as donors by the YcbB LDT although this was not observed. Thus, the absence of old→new 3→3 cross-linked Tri→Tetra dimer indicates that YcbB discriminates neo-synthesized tetrapeptide stems (used as donors) from existing tetrapeptide stems (used as acceptors) by an unknown mechanism that does not depend upon the structure of the disaccharide-peptide unit but upon the presence of the donor in a neo-synthesized glycan chain and of the acceptor in the existing peptidoglycan.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the absence of old→new dimers for YcbB-catalyzed reactions.

claim: The absence of old→new 3→3 cross-linked Tri→Tri dimers could be accounted for by the same mechanism that discriminates new from old tetrapeptide stems.
source: The absence of old→new 3→3 cross-linked Tri→Tri dimers could be accounted for by the same mechanism.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pattern observed for Tri→Tetra dimers.

claim: The Tri→Tri and Tetra→Tri dimers formed by YcbB and PBPs, respectively, were almost exclusively of the new→old type at early times after the medium switch (i.e. ≤20 min).
source: Kinetic analyses revealed that the Tri→Tri and Tetra→Tri dimers formed by YcbB and PBPs, respectively, were almost exclusively of the new→old type at early times after the medium switch (i.e. ≤20 min) (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: This is an observation from the kinetic analysis, illustrated in Figure 7A and B.

claim: Tri→Tetra and Tetra→Tetra dimers were mixtures of new→new and new→old types of dimers at early times after the medium switch.
source: In contrast, Tri→Tetra and Tetra→Tetra (formed by YcbB and PBPs; Figure 7C and D, respectively), which contained a tetrapeptide stem at the acceptor position, were mixtures of new→new and new→old types of dimers at early times after the medium switch.
evidence: This is an observation from the kinetic analysis, illustrated in Figure 7C and D.

claim: Incubation for longer time periods resulted in an increase in the proportion of new→new isotopologues for all types of dimers.
source: Incubation for longer time periods resulted in an increase in the proportion of new→new isotopologues for all types of dimers.
evidence: This is an observation from the kinetic analysis.

claim: The increase in new→new dimers was expected since serial and independent insertions of glycan strands at the same location result in the formation of new→new dimers.
source: This increase was expected since serial and independent insertions of glycan strands at the same location result in the formation of new→new dimers.
evidence: This is an explanation for the observed increase in new→new dimers.

claim: The increase in new→new dimers was more rapid for dimers containing a tetrapeptide stem at the acceptor position.
source: Note that this increase was more rapid for dimers containing a tetrapeptide stem at the acceptor position, as observed for tetrapeptide-containing monomers.
evidence: This is an observation from the kinetic analysis.

claim: The difference in the rate of increase of new→new dimers reflects the delayed formation of tripeptide stems from tetrapeptide stems by cleavage of D-Ala4 by the L,D-carboxypeptidase activity of YcbB.
source: As described above, this difference reflects the delayed formation of tripeptide stems from tetrapeptide stems by cleavage of D-Ala4 by the L,D-carboxypeptidase activity of YcbB.
evidence: This is an explanation for the observed difference in kinetics.

claim: The kinetics of formation of isotopologues containing a tripeptide stem at the acceptor position were similar for the Tri→Tri and Tetra→Tri dimers generated by YcbB and PBPs, respectively.
source: Together, the results shown in Figure 7 revealed that the kinetics of formation of isotopologues containing a tripeptide stem at the acceptor position were similar for the Tri→Tri and Tetra→Tri dimers generated by YcbB and PBPs, respectively.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the kinetic analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: The kinetics of formation of dimers containing a tetrapeptide stem at the acceptor position were similar for the Tri→Tetra and Tetra→Tetra generated by YcbB and PBPs, respectively.
source: Likewise, the kinetics of formation of dimers containing a tetrapeptide stem at the acceptor position were similar for the Tri→Tetra and Tetra→Tetra generated by YcbB and PBPs, respectively.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the kinetic analysis.

claim: Distinct kinetics were observed between dimers containing a stem tripeptide or tetrapeptide in the acceptor position irrespective of the transpeptidase responsible for their formation.
source: In contrast, distinct kinetics were observed between dimers containing a stem tripeptide or tetrapeptide in the acceptor position irrespective of the transpeptidase responsible for their formation (mainly new→old versus a mixture of new→new and new→old).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the kinetic analysis.

claim: The mode of insertion of peptidoglycan subunits depended upon the structure of the acceptor stem (tripeptide versus tetrapeptide) rather than upon the type of transpeptidase (PBPs versus YcbB).
source: Thus, the mode of insertion of peptidoglycan subunits depended upon the structure of the acceptor stem (tripeptide versus tetrapeptide) rather than upon the type of transpeptidase (PBPs versus YcbB).
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on the kinetic analysis.

claim: The newly formed peptidoglycan subunits are more rapidly incorporated in dimers containing a tetrapeptide stem in the acceptor position than in dimers containing a tripeptide stem at this position.
source: In addition, it is worth noting that the newly formed peptidoglycan subunits are more rapidly incorporated in dimers containing a tetrapeptide stem in the acceptor position than in dimers containing a tripeptide stem at this position.
evidence: This is an observation from the kinetic analysis.

claim: YcbB participates in the repair of peptidoglycan in a wild-type background.
source: Previous work concluded that YcbB also participates in the repair of peptidoglycan in a wild-type background (Morè et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous work, supported by citation.

claim: Peptidoglycan repair by YcbB requires glycosyltransferase and DDC activities provided by PBP1b and PBP6a, respectively.
source: In addition to YcbB, this process required glycosyltransferase and DDC activities provided by PBP1b and PBP6a, respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous work.

claim: Peptidoglycan repair proceeds by polymerization of new glycan chains that are cross-linked by PBPs.
source: This implies that peptidoglycan repair proceeds by polymerization of new glycan chains that are cross-linked by PBPs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the requirements for peptidoglycan repair.

claim: The mode of insertion of new peptidoglycan subunits delineated in the current study is fully compatible with the model of peptidoglycan repair.
source: It is worth noting that the mode of insertion of new peptidoglycan subunits delineated in the current study is fully compatible with this model since we detected only one type of 3→3 cross-linked dimers (new→old and not old→new).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observed dimer types.

claim: The absence of the six LDT genes greatly simplifies both the metabolic scheme for peptidoglycan cross-linking and the muropeptide rpHPLC profile in E. coli ∆6ldt.
source: Kinetic analyses of the insertion of peptidoglycan subunits was analyzed in E. coli ∆6ldt, a derivative of strain BW25113 that did not harbor any of the six E. coli LDT genes. The absence of the corresponding enzymes greatly simplifies both the metabolic scheme for peptidoglycan cross-linking and the muropeptide rpHPLC profile (Figure 8, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an observation about the ∆6ldt strain, illustrated in Figure 8 and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The rpHPLC profile of E. coli ∆6ldt contains only two main peaks, corresponding to the tetrapeptide monomer and the Tetra→Tetra dimer.
source: This profile contains only two main peaks, corresponding to the tetrapeptide monomer and the Tetra→Tetra dimer due to the absence of the formation of dimers containing 3→3 cross-links (LDT activity) and of monomers or dimers containing tripeptide stems (L,D-carboxypeptidase activity).
evidence: This is an observation from rpHPLC analysis of the ∆6ldt strain.

claim: The majority of the Tetra→Tetra dimers of the ∆6ldt strain were hybrids containing an unlabeled (de novo synthesized) tetrapeptide stem at the donor position and a labeled tetrapeptide stem (existing peptidoglycan) at the acceptor position.
source: The majority of the Tetra→Tetra dimers of the ∆6ldt strain were hybrids containing an unlabeled (de novo synthesized) tetrapeptide stem at the donor position and a labeled tetrapeptide stem (existing peptidoglycan) at the acceptor position.
evidence: This is an observation from MS analysis of the ∆6ldt strain.

claim: The pattern of dimer labeling in the ∆6ldt strain mainly fits the one-at-a time mode of insertion of newly synthesized glycan strands.
source: This pattern mainly fits the one-at-a time mode of insertion of newly synthesized glycan strands (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observed labeling pattern, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Exposure to aztreonam or mecillinam resulted in the morphological changes expected for the inhibition of septum formation (filamentation) or side wall synthesis (rounding), respectively.
source: Exposure to aztreonam or mecillinam resulted in the morphological changes expected for the inhibition of septum formation (filamentation) or side wall synthesis (rounding), respectively (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from microscopy analysis, illustrated in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: The kinetics of insertion of de novo synthesized subunits in the tetrapeptide monomers and in the Tetra→Tetra dimers were similar in the cultures containing aztreonam or no drug.
source: The kinetics of insertion of de novo synthesized subunits in the tetrapeptide monomers and in the Tetra→Tetra dimers were similar in the cultures containing aztreonam or no drug (Figure 8).
evidence: This is an observation from the kinetic analysis, illustrated in Figure 8.

claim: The pattern of dimer labeling in the presence of aztreonam or no drug corresponded to the one-at-a time mode of insertion of newly synthesized glycan strands since the new→new dimers were not abundant at the beginning of the kinetics.
source: The pattern corresponded to the one-at-a time mode of insertion of newly synthesized glycan strands since the new→new dimers were not abundant at the beginning of the kinetics.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observed labeling pattern.

claim: The new→new and new→old isotopologue dimers were both present in the cultures containing mecillinam, indicating that formation of the septum involves insertion of multiple strands at a time.
source: In contrast, the new→new and new→old isotopologue dimers were both present in the cultures containing mecillinam, indicating that formation of the septum involves insertion of multiple strands at a time.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observed labeling pattern in the presence of mecillinam.

claim: In the presence of ampicillin, the peptidoglycan of strain M1.5 was predominantly (ca. 99%) cross-linked by YcbB since the D,D-transpeptidase activity of PBPs was inhibited by the drug.
source: In the presence of ampicillin (16 µg/mL), the peptidoglycan of strain M1.5 was predominantly (ca. 99%) cross-linked by YcbB since the D,D-transpeptidase activity of PBPs was inhibited by the drug (Figure 9 and Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis of M1.5 grown in ampicillin, illustrated in Figure 9 and Supplementary file 1a.

claim: Inhibition of DDCs belonging to the PBP family prevented full hydrolysis of D-Ala5 since pentapeptide stems were detected both in monomers and in the acceptor position of dimers.
source: Inhibition of DDCs belonging to the PBP family prevented full hydrolysis of D-Ala5 since pentapeptide stems were detected both in monomers and in the acceptor position of dimers.
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis of M1.5 grown in ampicillin.

claim: New→new rather than new→old isotopologues were predominantly detected among dimers containing a tetrapeptide or a pentapeptide stem in the acceptor position in M1.5 grown in ampicillin.
source: New→new rather than new→old isotopologues were predominantly detected among dimers containing a tetrapeptide or a pentapeptide stem in the acceptor position.
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis of M1.5 grown in ampicillin.

claim: Dimers containing a tetrapeptide or pentapeptide stem in the acceptor position originate from neo-synthesized glycan chains cross-linked to each other.
source: These dimers originate from neo-synthesized glycan chains cross-linked to each other.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the new→new labeling pattern.

claim: The new→old isotopologues were more abundant than the new→new isotopologues in the Tri→Tetra dimers from the peptidoglycan of M1.5 grown in the absence of ampicillin at early times.
source: In contrast, the new→old isotopologues were more abundant than the new→new isotopologues in the Tri→Tetra dimers from the peptidoglycan of M1.5 grown in the absence of ampicillin at early times (Figure 7).
evidence: This is an observation from the kinetic analysis, illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: The difference in labeling patterns between M1.5 grown with and without ampicillin was not observed for the Tri→Tri dimers since the new→old isotopologues were prevalent for growth of M1.5 both in the presence or absence of ampicillin.
source: This difference was not observed for the Tri→Tri dimers since the new→old isotopologues were prevalent for growth of M1.5 both in the presence or absence of ampicillin.
evidence: This is an observation from the kinetic analysis.

claim: The prevalence of new→new dimers in M1.5 grown in ampicillin may be a consequence of the inhibition of the transpeptidase activity of PBPs by ampicillin that results in the uncoupling of the cross-linking and transglycosylation reactions.
source: The prevalence of new→new dimers may be a consequence of the inhibition of the transpeptidase activity of PBPs by ampicillin that results in the uncoupling of the cross-linking and transglycosylation reactions (Uehara and Park, 2008; Cho et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on established knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: Uncoupling of cross-linking and transglycosylation results in the accumulation of linear glycan strands that are eventually cross-linked to each other by YcbB.
source: This in turn results in the accumulation of linear glycan strands that are eventually cross-linked to each other by YcbB because they are not effectively degraded due to a mutation present in M1.5 that prevents production of lytic transglycosylase Slt70 (Voedts et al., 2021; Cho et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observed labeling pattern and knowledge of the M1.5 strain, supported by citations.

claim: The resulting new→new cross-linked material was almost exclusively connected to the existing peptidoglycan by the formation of Tri→Tri dimers because new→old isotopologues were only detected in this type of dimers.
source: The resulting new→new cross-linked material was almost exclusively connected to the existing peptidoglycan by the formation of Tri→Tri dimers because new→old isotopologues were only detected in this type of dimers.
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis of M1.5 grown in ampicillin.

claim: The acceptors of the cross-linking reactions in the existing peptidoglycan were tripeptides in M1.5 grown in ampicillin, whereas existing tetrapeptides also acted as acceptors in the absence of ampicillin.
source: This implies that the acceptors of the cross-linking reactions in the existing peptidoglycan were tripeptides, whereas existing tetrapeptides also acted as acceptors in the absence of ampicillin (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observed dimer types, with reference to Figure 7.

claim: The nearly exclusive use of existing tripeptides as acceptors in the presence of ampicillin could be accounted for by the fact that these tripeptides originate from cleavage of 3→3 cross-links liberating the tripeptide stems present in the donor position of the existing dimers.
source: The nearly exclusive use of existing tripeptides as acceptors in the presence of ampicillin could be accounted for by the fact that these tripeptides originate from cleavage of 3→3 cross-links liberating the tripeptide stems present in the donor position of the existing dimers.
evidence: This is a proposed explanation for the observed acceptor specificity.

claim: The model for peptidoglycan synthesis in M1.5 grown in ampicillin implies a cooperation between YcbB and an endopeptidase that provides the tripeptide acceptor substrate of the reaction by cleaving existing 3→3 cross-links.
source: This model implies a cooperation between YcbB and an endopeptidase that provides the tripeptide acceptor substrate of the reaction by cleaving existing 3→3 cross-links (Figure 12).
evidence: This is a proposed model illustrated in Figure 12.

claim: The endopeptidase that cooperates with YcbB could be MepK since this endopeptidase preferentially cleaves 3→3 cross-links in vitro, is essential for bacterial growth only in strains overproducing YcbB, and is not inhibited by ampicillin.
source: This enzyme could be MepK since this endopeptidase preferentially cleaves 3→3 cross-links in vitro, is essential for bacterial growth only in strains overproducing YcbB, and is not inhibited by ampicillin (Voedts et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a proposed identification of the endopeptidase based on its known properties, supported by citation.

claim: According to the model, the reactions catalyzed by MepK and YcbB are concerted rather than sequential.
source: According to this model, the reactions catalyzed by MepK and YcbB are concerted rather than sequential.
evidence: This is a feature of the proposed model.

claim: The mode of expansion of the peptidoglycan network in M1.5 grown in ampicillin differs from the 'make-before-break' models that postulate that neo-synthesized glycan strands are cross-linked to free stem peptides of the existing peptidoglycan prior to the cleavage of existing cross-links.
source: This mode of expansion of the peptidoglycan network differs from the 'make-before-break' models that postulate that neo-synthesized glycan strands are cross-linked to free stem peptides of the existing peptidoglycan prior to the cleavage of existing cross-links.
evidence: This is a conclusion about how the proposed model differs from existing models.

claim: In the absence of ampicillin, the hydrolysis of 4→3 cross-links by endopeptidases belonging to the PBP family could generate tetrapeptide acceptors in addition to the tripeptide acceptors exclusively used in the presence of the drug.
source: In the absence of ampicillin, the hydrolysis of 4→3 cross-links by endopeptidases belonging to the PBP family could generate tetrapeptide acceptors in addition to the tripeptide acceptors exclusively used in the presence of the drug.
evidence: This is a proposed explanation for the difference in acceptor usage with and without ampicillin.

claim: Pulse labeling with radioactive DAP suffers from four major limitations that are not encountered in the stable isotope labeling strategy.
source: Pulse labeling with radioactive DAP suffers from four major limitations that are not encountered in our labeling strategy.
evidence: This is a comparison of the new method with the previous radioactive DAP method.

claim: Optimization of radioactive DAP incorporation requires mutations that prevent endogenous DAP synthesis (lysA) and conversion of DAP to L-Lys (dapF).
source: First, optimization of radioactive DAP incorporation requires mutations that prevent endogenous DAP synthesis (lysA) and conversion of DAP to L-Lys (dapF) (Burman and Park, 1984; Glauner and Höltje, 1990; Goodell, 1985a; Goodell and Schwarz, 1985b; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the radioactive DAP method, supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Starvation prior to the addition of radiolabeled DAP was used to minimize the lag between the addition of radioactive DAP into the culture medium and its incorporation into peptidoglycan.
source: Starvation prior to the addition of radiolabeled DAP was used to minimize the lag between the addition of radioactive DAP into the culture medium and its incorporation into peptidoglycan (Glauner and Höltje, 1990; Burman and Park, 1984).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the radioactive DAP method, supported by citations.

claim: Depleting the intracellular DAP pool compromised the integrity of the peptidoglycan layer, affected cell morphology, and reduced turnover.
source: However, depleting the intracellular DAP pool compromised the integrity of the peptidoglycan layer (Burman et al., 1983b), affected cell morphology (Verwer and Nanninga, 1980), and reduced turnover (Burman et al., 1983b).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the effects of DAP depletion, supported by citations.

claim: The stable isotope labeling scheme is not affected by the confounding factors associated with DAP depletion since it does not require any metabolic engineering.
source: Our labeling scheme is not affected by these confounding factors since it does not require any metabolic engineering.
evidence: This is a claimed advantage of the new method.

claim: The radioactive DAP labeling procedures are unable to discriminate between muropeptides originating from the existing peptidoglycan, from the recycled L-Ala-D-iGlu-DAP tripeptide, or from the existing UDP-MurNAc-pentapeptide pool.
source: A second limitation of the DAP labeling procedures is their inability to discriminate between muropeptides originating from the existing peptidoglycan, from the recycled L-Ala-D-iGlu-DAP tripeptide, or from the existing UDP-MurNAc-pentapeptide pool, because all of them contain non-radioactive DAP.
evidence: This is a limitation of the radioactive DAP method identified by the authors.

claim: The stable isotope labeling procedure easily discriminates between muropeptides from existing peptidoglycan, recycled tripeptide, and the UDP-MurNAc-pentapeptide pool since they correspond to different isotopologues.
source: In contrast, our procedure easily discriminates between these three types of muropeptides since they correspond to different isotopologues, namely uniformly labeled subunits and hybrids h2 and h3, respectively (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a claimed advantage of the new method, illustrated in Figure 4.

claim: The h2 and h3 hybrids are likely to contribute to the lag phase observed for the incorporation of radioactive DAP into peptidoglycan in previous reports.
source: The latter hybrids are likely to contribute to the lag phase observed for the incorporation of radioactive DAP into peptidoglycan in previous reports (Glauner and Höltje, 1990; Burman and Park, 1984).
evidence: This is an interpretation of previous observations based on the current findings, supported by citations.

claim: A lag phase was observed when h2 and h3 hybrids containing [13C]- and [15N]-labeled DAP were excluded from the dataset.
source: Accordingly, a lag phase was observed in our study when h2 and h3 hybrids containing [13C]- and [15N]-labeled DAP were excluded from the dataset (Figure 10).
evidence: This is an observation from the current study, illustrated in Figure 10.

claim: The radioactive DAP labeling procedures provide access only to the average radioactivity content of donor and acceptor stem peptides.
source: A third limitation of the radioactive DAP labeling procedures for ADRR determination originates from the fact that they provide access only to the average radioactivity content of donor and acceptor stem peptides.
evidence: This is a limitation of the radioactive DAP method identified by the authors.

claim: The stable isotope labeling procedure provides direct access to the structure of dimers enabling identification of new→new, new→old, old→new, and old→old dimers based on differences in mass and fragmentation patterns.
source: Our procedure is richer in information because it provides direct access to the structure of dimers enabling identification of new→new, new→old, old→new, and old→old dimers based on differences in mass and fragmentation patterns.
evidence: This is a claimed advantage of the new method.

claim: Exploring peptidoglycan recycling by the radioactive DAP labeling procedures requires use of specific mutants and study designs.
source: The fourth limitation stems from the fact that exploring peptidoglycan recycling by the radioactive DAP labeling procedures requires use of specific mutants and study designs. For example, Jacobs et al., 1994, used mutants deficient in the production of the AmpG and Opp permeases in which peptidoglycan fragments are not recycled in the cytoplasm but released in the culture medium (Jacobs et al., 1994).
evidence: This is a limitation of the radioactive DAP method, supported by citation.

claim: The stable isotope labeling approach enables investigating peptidoglycan recycling and the mode of peptidoglycan expansion in a single experiment in the absence of any metabolic perturbation.
source: In contrast, our approach enables investigating peptidoglycan recycling and the mode of peptidoglycan expansion in a single experiment in the absence of any metabolic perturbation since it does not require altering the recycling pathway and is solely based on the determination of the structure of peptidoglycan fragments.
evidence: This is a claimed advantage of the new method.

claim: In the presence of aztreonam, the ADRNS for side wall synthesis was 0.14, 5 min after the medium switch.

claim: The results are in agreement with previous analyzes that have shown single-strand insertion of newly synthesized peptidoglycan into the side wall versus insertion of multiple strands for septal peptidoglycan synthesis.

source: In the absence of β-lactam, E. coli M1.5 relied both on the D,D-transpeptidase activity of PBPs and the LDT activity of YcbB for peptidoglycan cross-linking, leading to a high peptidoglycan content in both 4→3 (56%) and 3→3 (44%) cross-linked dimers (Supplementary file 1a).

source: Cho et al., 2014 proposed that the antibacterial activity of β-lactams does not merely rely on a loss of function, that is, the inactivation of the D,D-transpeptidase activity of PBPs by acylation of their catalytic Ser residue, but by inducing a toxic malfunctioning of the peptidoglycan biosynthesis machinery.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous work, supported by citation.

claim: The toxic malfunctioning of peptidoglycan biosynthesis involves uncoupling of transglycosylation and transpeptidation, accumulation of polymerized glycan chains, and their degradation by lytic transglycosylase Slt70.
source: This involves uncoupling of transglycosylation and transpeptidation, accumulation of polymerized glycan chains, and their degradation by lytic transglycosylase Slt70 (Banzhaf et al., 2012; Cho et al., 2014; Uehara and Park, 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous work, supported by citations.

claim: The futile cycle of glycan chain polymerization and degradation depletes resources and prevents bacterial growth.

evidence: This is an inference based on the futile cycle model.

source: This indicates that formation of 3→3 cross-links by YcbB is sufficient to stimulate peptidoglycan degradation in the absence of β-lactams.

claim: E. coli M1.5 is a derivative of E. coli BW25113 harboring plasmid pJEH12 for IPTG-inducible expression of the ycbB LDT gene, deletions of the erfK, ynhG, ycfS, and ybiS LDT genes, a 13 bp deletion lowering the translation level of the gene encoding the isoleucyl-tRNA synthase (IleRS), and an insertion of IS1 in gene sltY encoding lytic transglycosylase Slt70.
source: E. coli M1.5 (Hugonnet et al., 2016; Voedts et al., 2021) is a derivative of E. coli BW25113 (Datsenko and Wanner, 2000) harboring (i) plasmid pJEH12 for IPTG-inducible expression of the ycbB LDT gene, (ii) deletions of the erfK, ynhG, ycfS, and ybiS LDT genes, (iii) a 13 bp deletion lowering the translation level of the gene encoding the isoleucyl-tRNA synthase (IleRS) thereby increasing synthesis of the (p)ppGpp alarmone, and (iv) an insertion of IS1 in gene sltY encoding lytic transglycosylase Slt70 thereby promoting growth in the presence of ampicillin in liquid media (Voedts et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a description of the M1.5 strain, supported by citations.

source: Upon induction of ycbB by IPTG, E. coli M1.5 expresses high-level resistance to ampicillin and ceftriaxone following production of YcbB.
evidence: This is a description of the M1.5 strain phenotype.

source: E. coli ∆6ldt is a derivative of strain BW25113 obtained by deletion of the six LDT genes present in E. coli (erfK, ynhG, ycfS, ybiS, yafK, and ycbB) (Magnet et al., 2007; Magnet et al., 2008; Montón Silva et al., 2018; Morè et al., 2019).
